prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the standing person roughly 0.7–1.2 m in front of the camera wearer, with the counter edge and nearby surfaces within about 0.2–0.6 m; the display case is approximately 0.8–1.5 m away and beside the person. Across the five frames, the person remains at a similar distance while shifting from left-of-centre toward the right as the camera viewpoint turns, and parts of the person overlap the display case in depth. Bright foreground regions clarify that the counter is nearer than both the person and display, which is harder to judge from RGB alone. Exact distances are unreliable because monocular depth has no metric scale, dark regions merge the person with the background, and bright surfaces near the lower edge appear saturated or geometrically distorted.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates one person in front of the camera and a display case labelled “tv” beside them, while a small counter object labelled “keyboard” appears in the first three frames within roughly 0.3–0.8 m of the camera wearer. It makes object boundaries and occlusion order clearer than RGB: the person is generally nearer than the display, partly blocks it in some frames, and is partially cropped at the top throughout. From frames 1–5, the person shifts from the left half through the centre toward the right relative to the camera, while the display moves from right to left in the image as the viewpoint turns; the two remain roughly within an arm’s length of each other. The map is unreliable in class identity and shape: the display case is mislabelled as a TV, the small object may not be a keyboard, masks omit thin limbs and carried items, and the fourth-frame display changes colour or instance identity unexpectedly.
descriptions.pose: The pose map shows the person’s torso and arms facing generally toward the camera wearer in frames 2–4, with the head above the torso and both hands held low in front of the body, about 0.7–1.2 m from the camera. The hand keypoints cluster close together near waist or counter height, indicating that the hands are within the person’s own arm’s reach and near the foreground counter; in frame 1 only hand fragments are detected, and in frame 5 most of the body and one hand are missing or out of view. Across the middle frames, the skeleton shifts right-to-left within its frame region and changes angle slightly, supporting modest body turning rather than a large approach or retreat; head orientation is too incomplete to determine reliably whether the person looks directly at the camera wearer. Compared with RGB, the map exposes approximate joint arrangement and hand proximity, but it is highly unreliable where joints float above the head, limbs connect incorrectly, hands overlap, or cropping and occlusion cause missing keypoints.
